title: Who wears them
hook: traditionally men from bar mitzvah; in many non-Orthodox communities women wear them too

segments.voice: Yesterday, erusin: three turns around the finger, like a ring, with Hosea's promise. Your line was like a ring. Which quality did you carry? Today, the last day on tefillin, and a real question. Day one hundred forty-three.

Two synagogues stand on the same street. It's the same weekday morning in both. In the first, the men's section is full of arms wrapped in black straps, fathers next to sons, a boy of twelve putting them on for the first time with his grandfather watching. The women pray on their own side, without tefillin. In the second, a woman in her forties is winding a strap around her arm, next to a teenage girl doing the same. Both rooms are praying the same prayers. Each follows a reading it has thought through. And both are Jewish.
screen: `TWO SYNAGOGUES, ONE STREET.` → `A BOY AND HIS GRANDFATHER.` → `A WOMAN WINDING A STRAP.`

segments.voice: Here's how it developed. Traditional Jewish law says Jewish men are obligated to wear tefillin from bar mitzvah, which the Mishnah puts at thirteen, the age of commandments. In some communities, boys start practicing a little before. Women, in traditional law, are exempt. Not forbidden, exempt, because of a general rule that women are exempt from positive commandments tied to a set time, and tefillin are worn by day. Then there's a surprising line in the Talmud: Michal, the daughter of King Saul, wore tefillin, and the sages did not protest. Rabbis over the centuries argued about what to make of that. Some said a woman may choose to take on the practice; later codes, like the Rema's notes to the Shulchan Aruch, discouraged it. Today, communities answer differently, and each has its reasons. Orthodox communities generally keep the traditional practice: men wear tefillin, and women don't. Conservative Judaism teaches that women may take on the commandment, and its law committee has ruled that women can be equally obligated, so in many Conservative synagogues, women wear tefillin. In Reform and other liberal communities, tefillin are a personal choice for anyone, and some people of all genders wear them, while many don't wear them at all. There are also Jews who wear them only now and then, and outreach volunteers on city streets who offer to help a passing Jewish man put them on for a minute. What's worth noticing is that all of these communities care about the same verse and the same boxes. They differ over who is bound by it. Learning that a custom isn't yours is not the same as thinking it's wrong.
screen: `MEN, FROM BAR MITZVAH.` · `WOMEN: EXEMPT, NOT FORBIDDEN.` · `MICHAL WORE TEFILLIN.` · `EACH COMMUNITY ANSWERS.` · then, large: `CUSTOMS DIFFER, RESPECT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one custom from a community not your own. Later, look one up, or ask someone. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of a practice you've seen done differently from how you do it, or from how you'd do it. A holiday, a meal, a way of praying, a way of mourning. Before you judge it, picture the people who love it. Ask what it means to them. Hold that question for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Tefillin, the black straps and boxes traditionally worn by Jewish men from bar mitzvah, and today by women too in many non-Orthodox communities.
Your line: customs differ, respect holds. Today, when you meet a way of doing things that isn't yours, ask about it before you decide what you think. Day one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: In Orthodox communities, men and boys from bar mitzvah wear tefillin each weekday morning. In many Conservative and liberal communities, women may wear them too, and in Reform communities wearing them is a personal choice.

fork.setup: you're visiting a friend's synagogue, and they do tefillin differently from what you grew up with. what do you do?
options: tell them they're doing it wrong.
ask what the custom means to them.
fork.reveal: there's no single right answer in the text. but every community here cares about the same verse; asking is how respect starts.

trapdoor: what you thought: tefillin are for men.
what it means: traditionally men from bar mitzvah; women exempt but not forbidden; communities today answer differently.
what a scholar hears: Kiddushin 33b–34a on time-bound commandments; Eruvin 96a on Michal; Conservative movement rulings (CJLS) on women's obligation.

sources.ref: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 38:3 with Rema
